title: Know what interviewers are really testing in the 8 fit questions consultancies ask most
description: The fit questions you are most likely to be asked in a consulting interview, what each one is really testing, and how to answer.
hook: These are the fit questions you are most likely to be asked, and what the interviewer is really trying to learn from each one.
body:
1. Tell me about yourself

This is your story in about 90 seconds, not your CV read aloud. A simple shape works well: where you started and what drove your choices, two or three moments you are proud of, and why consulting and this firm make sense now. End on the present, so the conversation flows into the next question. Practise it out loud until it sounds like you talking, not reciting.

2. Why consulting? Why this firm?

Interviewers want proof you have done real homework. Mention people you have spoken to at the firm and what struck you, a practice area or type of work that genuinely interests you, and how it connects to what you have done before. Avoid lines that could appear on any firm's website, like "I want to solve interesting problems".

3. A time you led through difficulty

They are asking whether people follow you when things are hard. Pick a moment where something went wrong or a team was stuck, and be specific about what you did: the conversation you had, the decision you made, how you kept people going. Finish with the result and what you would do the same, or differently, next time.

4. A failure

Choose a real failure that mattered, not a disguised strength. Own your part in it clearly, without blaming others. Most of your time should go on what you learned and, importantly, what you now do differently. Interviewers are looking for honesty and growth, and a candidate who can talk about failure calmly is reassuring.

5. Persuading without authority

Consultants constantly persuade people they do not manage, including clients. Tell a story where you changed someone's mind. The key detail interviewers listen for: did you understand the other person's position and why they held it? Show how you used that, whether through data, a small test or finding common ground.

6. Your biggest impact

Pick the achievement where you made the clearest difference, and put a number on it if you can: money saved, time cut, people helped. Then make your own role obvious. "We" is fine for the team, but say what you personally did that would not have happened without you.

7. A time you took initiative

They want to see that you start things nobody asked you to. A good story begins with something you noticed, a problem or an opportunity, then what you did about it without waiting for permission, and what changed as a result. Small and real is better than grand and vague.

8. Your weakness

Pick a real weakness that would not stop you doing the job, explain how it has shown up, and spend most of your answer on what you actively do to manage it. "I'm a perfectionist" sounds rehearsed. Something like "I used to take on too much myself; now I agree priorities with my manager at the start of each week" sounds honest and self-aware.

One set of stories, many questions

You do not need a separate story for every question. Six to eight well-prepared stories, each with a clear situation, what you did, the result and what you learned, will cover almost anything. The fit interview guide shows how to build them.
outro: Read it once, then try it on a practice case today while it is fresh. One real attempt teaches more than three re-reads. Build and save your stories in the free fit stories builder.
